newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AWB boosts Australia wheat estimate to 22 m/t.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AWB boosts Australia wheat estimate to 22 m/t.

text.p: The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) has increased its estimate of Australia's 1996/97 wheat crop to 22 million tonnes from its previous estimate of 21.5 million.
The revision, contained in the AWB's latest weekly market report, follows trade talk in recent weeks that the crop could be as much as 23 to 24 million tonnes.
The boost makes the AWB's forecast highest among official and professional private forecasters.
The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) forecast is 21.3 million tonnes while private forecaster Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd forecasts 21.37 million.
The AWB also publicly released price details for the first time on last week's sale to Pakistan.
An additional 180,000 tonnes sold to Pakistan was priced at around A$193.00 a tonne, AWB said.

Private traders said last week the price was set at US$156.285 a tonne. The AWB's weekly report revises an earlier statement by the board that the Pakistan sale involved 112,000 tonnes of Australian Standard White.
The U.S. sale of 135,000 tonnes of white wheat to Pakistan in the same tender was priced at A$192.00 a tonne, AWB said in its weekly report.

The AWB gave no price details in its weekly report on last week's 1.5 million tonne wheat sale to Iran, although chairman Trevor Flugge told Reuters on Friday it was priced at about the same level as wheat in the latest Pakistan sale.
The AWB said in the report that there was the possibility of doing still more business with Iran.

In other international news, Brazil was reported to have bought Argentine wheat at A$183.00 a tonne with Argentine wheat offered to the market at A$198.00 a tonne and French wheat offered at A$191.00 a tonne, AWB said.
This was the second consecutive week Argentina's offered price had risen, AWB said.

On the Australian domestic scene, AWB said three dry weeks in Queensland were raising questions about potential sorghum supplies. While conditions remained good in the south, the crop was under pressure in central Queensland.
Sorghum prices had yet to show any reaction in Queensland or New South Wales (NSW), it said.
Feed barley prices remained firm and an indication of the strength of the feed grain market was increasing interest in triticale in NSW, it said.
In contrast, feed wheat prices were being driven by the dairy industry. The milling wheat market remained quiet with bids for ASW dropping by A$7.00 a tonne in NSW, it said. Wheat Shipping:
